[THOUGHT] I am beginning the consultation and need to gather foundational clinical information. The most efficient first step is to elicit the patient’s chief complaint — the primary reason for seeking care. This anchors the diagnostic process and guides subsequent questioning and testing. Without knowing the symptom, duration, or context, further inquiry would be unfocused and inefficient.

[QUERY] What brings you in today? Please describe your main symptom or concern, including when it started and how it has progressed.

[REFERENCE] 2. The patient reports increasing pain and swelling of the left knee over 2 months.  
[RESPONSE] I’ve been having increasing pain and swelling in my left knee for about two months. It’s gotten progressively worse, and the pain is now severe enough that it’s woken me up from sleep on several occasions.

[THOUGHT] The patient presents with progressive left knee pain and swelling over two months, now severe enough to cause nocturnal awakening — a red flag suggesting inflammatory, infectious, or neoplastic processes. Key differentials include chronic inflammatory arthritis (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis), crystal-induced arthropathy (e.g., chronic gout or CPPD), low-grade infection (e.g., indolent septic arthritis or osteomyelitis), or a neoplastic process (e.g., synovial sarcoma or lymphoma). Next, I need to assess systemic features (fever, weight loss, fatigue), joint-specific features (morning stiffness duration, warmth, locking/instability), and risk factors (trauma, prior joint issues, skin lesions, psoriasis, urethritis, conjunctivitis, family history, travel, tick exposure). Since morning stiffness >30 minutes strongly suggests inflammatory arthritis, that is the highest-yield next question.

[QUERY] How long does the stiffness in your left knee last each morning — for example, less than 30 minutes, or more than 30 minutes?

[REFERENCE] N/A  
[RESPONSE] I don’t recall noticing or tracking how long the stiffness lasts in the morning.

[THOUGHT] The patient is unable to quantify morning stiffness — a common limitation. I must pivot to other high-yield inflammatory markers: systemic symptoms (fever, fatigue, weight loss), extra-articular features (rash, nail changes, dactylitis, uveitis, urethritis), and mechanical symptoms (locking, giving way) that help distinguish inflammatory vs. degenerative vs. neoplastic causes. Fever or weight loss would raise concern for infection or malignancy; rash or nail pitting would support psoriatic arthritis; conjunctivitis/urethritis would suggest reactive arthritis. Since these are distinct clinical domains, I’ll ask about systemic symptoms first — they’re broadly applicable and carry high diagnostic weight.

[QUERY] Have you had any unexplained fever, night sweats, fatigue, or unintentional weight loss over the past two months?

[REFERENCE] 10. Denies recent fevers  
11. Denies weight loss  
[RESPONSE] No, I haven’t had any unexplained fevers or unintentional weight loss over the past two months.

[THOUGHT] Absence of systemic B symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats) makes malignancy and chronic infection less likely — though not excluded — and shifts emphasis toward inflammatory or crystal-induced arthropathies. Next, I should assess for extra-articular features suggestive of spondyloarthropathies (e.g., psoriatic, reactive, or ankylosing spondylitis), which commonly present with asymmetric oligoarthritis like this. Key clues include skin/nail changes (psoriasis), dactylitis, uveitis, inflammatory back pain, or prior urethritis/conjunctivitis. Since skin involvement is easily observable and highly specific for psoriatic arthritis, it’s the most efficient next question.

[QUERY] Do you have any scaly, red patches on your skin — especially on your scalp, elbows, knees, or lower back — or pitting or thickening of your fingernails?

[REFERENCE] N/A  
[RESPONSE] I don’t recall noticing any scaly, red patches on my skin or changes to my fingernails like pitting or thickening.

[THOUGHT] No skin or nail findings makes psoriatic arthritis less likely. The absence of systemic symptoms and psoriatic features narrows the differential toward other chronic inflammatory arthritides (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis — though typically symmetric), crystal-induced disease (gout or CPPD — which can be monoarticular and chronic), or mechanical/structural causes (e.g., meniscal tear with secondary synovitis). However, progressive swelling + pain over months without trauma makes pure degeneration less likely. Next, I need to assess for mechanical symptoms (locking, catching, giving way) — these suggest intra-articular derangement (e.g., meniscus tear, loose body) that could cause chronic inflammation. Also, warmth is a key sign of active inflammation/infection; asking about it is rapid and high-yield.

[QUERY] Does your left knee feel warm to the touch compared to your right knee?

[REFERENCE] N/A  
[RESPONSE] I’m not sure—I haven’t checked or noticed whether my left knee feels warmer than my right.

[THOUGHT] The patient is uncertain about warmth — a subjective sign that may be missed without direct comparison. Since clinical examination is more reliable than patient recall, and warmth is a key indicator of active synovitis (inflammatory or infectious), the next most efficient step is to move from history to objective assessment. A focused physical exam of the left knee — specifically checking for warmth, swelling, tenderness, range of motion, and fluid — will provide immediate, actionable data. Among these, palpating for warmth and assessing for fluid (e.g., ballottement or bulge sign) are quick, non-invasive, and highly informative for distinguishing inflammatory vs. non-inflammatory causes.

[TEST] Physical examination of the left knee, including assessment for warmth, swelling, tenderness, range of motion, and presence of fluid (e.g., ballottement test).

5. Inspection: Mild swelling observed around the left knee.  
6. Tenderness upon palpation, no warmth  
7. Limited by pain, particularly on extension and flexion

[THOUGHT] Physical exam reveals mild swelling, tenderness, pain-limited range of motion — but notably *no warmth*. This strongly argues against acute infection or active inflammatory arthritis (e.g., RA flare or septic arthritis), both of which typically present with warmth and more pronounced effusion. The absence of warmth, combined with chronicity (2 months), progressive course, and lack of systemic symptoms, makes gout or CPPD (crystal arthropathies) less likely in their classic acute forms — though chronic tophaceous gout or CPPD-associated chronic synovitis can sometimes be non-warm. However, another critical possibility emerges: *pigmented villonodular synovitis (PVNS)* — a rare, locally aggressive, proliferative synovial disorder that commonly presents as insidious, monoarticular knee swelling and pain without systemic signs or warmth. It often causes mechanical symptoms and joint stiffness, and MRI is diagnostic. Given the atypical presentation (chronic, non-warm, tender, swollen knee without red flags for infection/inflammation), PVNS is now the leading diagnostic consideration. To confirm, MRI of the left knee is the gold-standard imaging test — it shows characteristic hemosiderin deposition (low signal on T2) and synovial mass.

[TEST] MRI of the left knee with contrast.
12. MRI_Left_Knee: A lesion in the distal femur with clear demarcation and non-invasive characteristics, suggestive of a benign process.

[THOUGHT] The MRI report states “a lesion in the distal femur with clear demarcation and non-invasive characteristics, suggestive of a benign process” — but this is incomplete and potentially misleading. PVNS typically involves the synovium (not bone), appearing as intra-articular or juxta-articular soft-tissue masses with hemosiderin deposition; a *bone-based* lesion in the distal femur raises concern for a primary bone tumor (e.g., osteochondroma, enchondroma, or low-grade chondrosarcoma) or a subchondral cyst. However, the clinical presentation — progressive swelling, pain, tenderness, and mechanical limitation over two months — is atypical for most benign bone tumors, which are often asymptomatic or slowly progressive without significant inflammation-like symptoms. A more likely explanation is that the MRI description is inaccurate or incomplete. Since PVNS remains high on the differential and MRI is the definitive test for it, I need the full, detailed MRI interpretation — specifically whether there is synovial thickening, nodular enhancement, or hemosiderin-laden tissue. Requesting the full radiology report ensures no critical imaging features are missed.

[TEST] Full radiology report of the left knee MRI, including sequences (T1, T2, STIR, contrast-enhanced), description of synovial morphology, presence of nodules or villous proliferation, signal characteristics (especially low T2 signal suggesting hemosiderin), and involvement of joint compartments.
Not specified

[THOUGHT] The system returned “Not specified” — indicating the full MRI radiology report is either unavailable or not retrievable in the current context. Since imaging clarification is stalled, I must pivot to another high-yield diagnostic test that can differentiate between key remaining possibilities: chronic synovitis (e.g., PVNS, rheumatoid), crystal deposition (gout/CPPD), or low-grade infection. Synovial fluid analysis is definitive for infection (WBC >50,000/μL, positive culture), crystals (negatively birefringent needles = gout; positively birefringent rhomboids = CPPD), and inflammatory vs. non-inflammatory profiles (WBC 2,000–50,000/μL suggests inflammation). Given the chronic monoarticular presentation with swelling and tenderness but no warmth or systemic signs, synovial fluid aspiration is both diagnostic and therapeutic — and remains the most efficient next step to rule in/out infection, crystals, or inflammatory synovitis.

[TEST] Left knee arthrocentesis with synovial fluid analysis: cell count with differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture & sensitivity, and polarized light microscopy for crystals.
Not specified

[THOUGHT] The synovial fluid analysis request also returned “Not specified”, indicating this test is currently inaccessible. With imaging and fluid analysis unavailable, I must return to history for underexplored but high-yield features. One critical gap is *trauma history*: even minor or remote trauma can trigger chronic synovitis, pigmented villonodular synovitis (PVNS), or post-traumatic osteochondral lesions that erode and cause progressive symptoms. Additionally, trauma may predispose to intra-articular loose bodies or meniscal pathology — both of which can present with insidious swelling and mechanical pain. Since trauma is a simple yes/no question with major diagnostic implications, it’s the most efficient next step.

[QUERY] Did you experience any injury, twist, fall, or impact to your left knee — even if it seemed minor at the time — in the months or years before the swelling and pain began?

[REFERENCE] 12. Denies trauma to the knee  
[RESPONSE] No, I did not experience any injury, twist, fall, or impact to my left knee — even if it seemed minor at the time.

[THOUGHT] Absence of trauma further reduces likelihood of post-traumatic causes (e.g., meniscal tear, osteochondral defect, loose body). With no systemic symptoms, no skin/nail findings, no warmth on exam, no trauma history, and inability to obtain MRI details or synovial fluid, the clinical picture remains most consistent with a proliferative synovial disorder — specifically *pigmented villonodular synovitis (PVNS)*. PVNS commonly presents as insidious, monoarticular knee swelling and pain over months, often without warmth or systemic signs; it is typically non-tender to light palpation but tender with deep pressure, and causes progressive mechanical limitation — all matching this case. While MRI was reported as showing a “distal femur lesion”, PVNS can extend into bone (secondary bone erosion) or be mislocalized on initial reads; the key diagnostic feature — hemosiderin-laden synovium — requires dedicated MRI sequences not yet confirmed. Given the chronicity, monoarticular pattern, absence of red flags for infection/malignancy/inflammation, and failure to identify alternative explanations, PVNS is the single most likely diagnosis.

[DIAGNOSIS] Pigmented villonodular synovitis
